title: Ministry Embellishment and the Heart of a Leader
author: Daniel Seabaugh
summary: Pastor Daniel Seabaugh addresses a temptation he sees across ministry leadership: embellishing impact so that congregants, volunteers and donors stay pleased and keep giving, serving and attending. He suggests the impulse often stems from a leader's desire to cover inadequacy or win approval, and insists that however much ministry deserves excellence, embellishment of any kind is dishonest and lacks integrity. The article's central move is an exposition of 1 Samuel 16, where Samuel passes over Jesse's impressive older sons and God chooses David, who was not even in the lineup because he was tending sheep. Seabaugh draws two lessons for leaders: that motives matter more than accomplishments, since leaders who polish the outside while neglecting the interior life eventually fall, and that worldly ways of assessing talent and impact can miss who is actually fit to lead. He closes by urging leaders neither to stretch the truth about their impact nor to place people in positions they have not been called to. Classified as Leadership because the operational target is integrity in how leaders report results and assess people, despite the explicitly Christian framing.
points: Seabaugh identifies inflating ministry impact to keep donors, volunteers and attenders engaged as a common leadership temptation rooted in insecurity or approval-seeking.
He separates excellence from embellishment: work can deserve our best while any exaggeration of results remains dishonest.
Leaders who fall have often 'polished the outside of the cup' while neglecting their interior life and trusting others' applause.
From David's selection in 1 Samuel 16 he argues that conventional talent assessment favors those who look the part and can overlook faithful people doing unimpressive work.
The closing charge pairs honesty about impact with care in appointments: do not stretch the truth, and do not place people in roles they are not fit for.
quotes: One unfortunate reality I’ve seen in ministry is the temptation to make things look better than they actually are. The temptation often plays out as embellishing ministry impact so that congregants, volunteers, and financial supporters are pleased and willing to continue giving, serving, and attending.

I’m guessing every leader falls prey to this temptation from time to time. Instead of being servants of God, we perform for people. Instead of relying on the power of God, we boast in our abilities and play to our strengths.

Ministry should be done with excellence, to be sure. Making disciples is a big deal. It’s sacred work that deserves our best. Yet, embellishment of any kind is dishonest and deceptive. It lacks integrity.

Many impactful leaders have fallen because they polished the outside of the cup while neglecting the inside. They paid little attention to their interior life and were deceived by the applause of others.
No, the problem lays with placing priority on outward appearances while paying little regard to the interior life—a life of humble, surrendered obedience.
Perhaps the lesson for all men and women in ministry is that God’s standard for leadership is, at times, different from our own. We have a worldly way of assessing talent and impact.
Let’s not stretch the truth of our impact or put people in positions whom God hasn’t called.
